new_statements.rule_in_words: The source characterises Salka Kambari (Tsishingini) as a two-level-tone language with light lexical tone load and a Salka-specific ban on word-initial High tone (nouns L-initial; imperative verbs mostly LH); it gives NO statement about the existence or location of word stress. The only occurrence of 'stress' in the book is an appendix heading 'Unstressed /u/' (p. 200, Auna Kambari/Tsikimba) describing a reduced root-final vowel before suffixes, which is not a stress-placement rule and not about the Salka variety.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone only: imperative verbs 'nearly always LH' with some LL exceptions (e.g. zama 'search'); no HH nouns; Salka lacks the H-initial noun patterns found in Auna/Agwara.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone patterns given for citation forms elicited in isolation (nouns with class prefix; verbs in the imperative); grammatical tone on verbs said to be redundant with subject-pronoun set. Phonology chapter treats the three Kambari co-languages together, flagging Salka-specific facts.
new_statements.identity_note: Naming trap: Crozier (1984, 1993) uses 'Cishingini'/'Kambari' for Central (Salka) Kambari = Glottolog tsis1238 / ISO tsw, whereas Stark (2004, 2010) uses 'Cishingini' for Agwara (Western) Kambari = cish1238 / asg and 'Tsishingini' for Salka (Blench & McGill 2012:9 make the same point; SIL archive files Crozier 1984 under tsw). Stark 2010 describes the three co-languages jointly (examples mostly Auna Kambari = Tsikimba, tsik1238) and flags Salka-specific facts, notably the ban on word-initial High tone; the 'Unstressed /u/' note (p. 200) is in the Auna Kambari (Tsikimba) orthography appendix, not Salka. Hoffmann 1965's 'Central Kambari' is Raba and Salka speech (tsw). The Rosetta extract of Alphabets of Africa is filed under asg but per Stark 2010:1.6.1 reflects Crozier's Salka-based work.

new_statements.quote: The language has two contrastive tone levels. [...] While contrastive tone can be established by careful elicitation of minimal pairs, the total number of tone pairs is very small (at most 15–20 pairs of words in each language), and in nearly all instances words coming from different word classes are involved [...] There is a small functional load for tone in Kambari. The mother-tongue speaker has a sense of ‘normal’ tone patterns for a word, similar to the sense of proper stress placement in English. [...] These factors allow a practical orthography that does not mark tone

'While contrastive tone can be established by careful elicitation of minimal pairs, the total number of tone pairs is very small (at most 15-20 pairs of words in each language), and in nearly all instances words coming from different wo…
new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Janie Stark 2010 statement (two level lexical tones, very small semantic/functional load, tone unmarked in orthography) and, like it, no word-stress statement; the catalog record itself has an empty rule. Adds the explicit count of minimal tone pairs (15-20 per co-language) and the noun/verb tone-pattern inventory, and states the description covers Tsishingini (Salka) along with Cishingini and Tsikimba.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kambari (all three co-languages, explicitly including Tsishingini/Salka; data illustrated with Agwara forms) has two contrastive level tones (noun patterns LL, HL, LHL, LLL; verbs LH) with a very small functional load (at most 15-20 minimal tone pairs per language), so the orthography leaves tone unmarked. The book gives no rule for word-stress placement and does not say whether stress is contrastive; 'stress' appears only in an analogy to English and in a passing remark (E.1.7, p. 101) that most VV syllables 'receive a single stress with slight temporal length'.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone of morphemes in context may differ from isolation tone but 'this tone variation is never the only variation in the phrase' and 'does not in and of itself carry semantic content' (E.2, p. 101). Pronunciation Guide p. xii: 'Tone plays a very small role in the semantic interpretation of spoken Kambari. The standard Kambari orthography does not mark tone'. E.1 p. 94: the phonological presentation 'is illustrated with Agwara Kambari data' but 'The three languages share the same phonemic inventory, word structures, and phonological processes.'
new_statements.identity_note: John Stark 2011 describes the Kambari cluster as three co-languages -- Cishingini (Agwara, asg), Tsikimba (Auna-Wara), Tsishingini (Salka, tsw = tsis1238) -- and illustrates the phonology appendix with Agwara (Cishingini) forms while stating the phonemic inventory, word structures, processes and tone system are shared by all three; the Pronunciation Guide notes Salka-specific free variation of [ɛ~e], [ɔ~o]. The tone statement is therefore cluster-wide rather than elicited specifically from Salka speakers.
